Executive Summary

The Serverless File Processing System (SFPS) is an event-driven AWS pipeline that validates uploaded files, extracts metadata, computes a SHA-256 checksum, and records the outcome of every object version in Amazon DynamoDB. A file placed under the incoming/ prefix of a private, versioned Amazon S3 bucket asynchronously invokes a single AWS Lambda function. The function validates the extension, size, content signature, and decodability of the file, extracts type-specific metadata, hashes the original bytes, and writes a deterministic processing record. Structured JSON logs go to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Failures that exhaust asynchronous retries are delivered to an Amazon SQS queue.

The project was built as a complete V1 rather than an architecture sketch. The repository contains the Lambda source, a pure validation layer, image and text processors, a SHA-256 helper, a pytest suite with moto-mocked AWS services, a requirements lock, and a manual AWS deployment guide. The function was deployed to the ap-south-1 region on Python 3.13 with the arm64 architecture, 512 MB of memory, and a 30-second timeout. The deployment package was built on Windows with Linux arm64 wheels, uploaded as a ZIP archive, and verified for layout and dependency versions.

The design concentrates on three properties that separate a working demo from a dependable processing pipeline. First, every read is pinned to the object version carried by the S3 event, so the bytes that are validated, hashed, and measured are the bytes identified by the record. Second, the DynamoDB write protocol uses conditional writes and a deterministic processing_id derived from the bucket, object key, and version ID, so duplicate deliveries cannot create a second logical record or overwrite a completed result. Third, failures are classified. Permanent validation failures become FAILED records and do not trigger retries; infrastructure failures are logged with sanitized frames, re-raised, retried by Lambda, and delivered to SQS when the retries are exhausted.

The evidence collected on 18 October 2026 shows the deployed system processing the planned acceptance inputs. The DynamoDB table held 25 records at the time of the scan: 10 COMPLETED and 15 FAILED. Those 25 records are not 25 independent test scenarios. They include two versions of the same sample image, seven zero-byte folder-marker records, and the positive and negative case-study fixtures. The captured SQS message shows the expected invocation envelope with condition RetriesExhausted, approximateInvokeCount 3, the original event under requestPayload, and a sanitized InfrastructureError in responsePayload. One successful PNG invocation was recorded at 89 ms of application processing, 150.13 ms of Lambda execution, and 117 MB of peak memory against a 512 MB configuration.

The automated suite was re-run for this case study: 135 tests passed in 48.66 seconds, Ruff reported no issues, and pip check found no broken requirements. The deployment archive contained 2,358 entries, measured 22,955,647 bytes compressed and 45,828,329 bytes uncompressed, placed handler.py at the archive root, used forward-slash entry names, and included eight aarch64 Pillow extension libraries with all eight runtime dependency versions matching requirements.txt.

The case study does not claim production-grade security, fault tolerance, or general performance. It does not claim that the 25 MiB memory and timeout boundary was measured on the deployed function, that every per-file error code is legible in the captured console views, or that any AWS cost figure is known beyond the pay-per-use model. Those gaps are listed with the evidence inventory and the outstanding tests. The value of the project lies in the combination of a working deployed pipeline, a failure model that distinguishes expected rejections from operational faults, and a documented trail that makes the claims checkable.

Project Highlights

WHAT THE PROJECT DEMONSTRATES
  • Event-driven flow from a private, versioned S3 bucket to a single Python 3.13 Lambda function and a DynamoDB processing table.
  • Validation order that rejects unsupported extensions before download, then checks size, content signature, image decodability, or strict UTF-8 text.
  • One deterministic DynamoDB record per S3 object version, protected by conditional writes and a skip-only-COMPLETED idempotency rule.
  • Metadata extraction for JPEG, PNG, and text, plus SHA-256 over the version-pinned original bytes.
  • Permanent validation failures recorded as FAILED without retries; infrastructure failures re-raised through Lambda's asynchronous retry path.
  • Structured JSON logs with allowlisted error messages and sanitized stack frames; 30-day log retention.
  • On-failure SQS destination confirmed by a captured invocation envelope with RetriesExhausted and approximateInvokeCount 3.
  • 135 automated tests, a clean Ruff run, and a verified Linux arm64 deployment archive built from Windows.

Abbreviations and Terminology

CHAPTER 1

Introduction

1.1 Background#

File processing is a routine backend task with a deceptive amount of detail. A system receives a file, decides whether it is acceptable, extracts information from it, stores the result, and tells an operator what happened. In a small prototype, a single script can do all of that. In an operational system, the same script has to handle duplicate deliveries, partial failures, large inputs, malformed content, security boundaries, retries, and the need to explain later why a particular file produced a particular record.

Traditional server-based processing puts a long-running worker in front of that problem. The worker polls a queue or watches a directory, keeps libraries loaded, and writes to a database. This model is familiar and can be efficient at sustained load. It also asks the team to manage capacity, patching, idle time, and failure recovery for a process that may receive only a few files an hour. A serverless model replaces the idle worker with an event source and a function that runs only when work arrives. The operational surface shrinks, but the correctness surface does not. The function still needs idempotency, bounded resource use, and a clear failure model.

SFPS explores that trade-off in a concrete AWS deployment. The project uses Amazon S3 as the source of truth for uploaded bytes, AWS Lambda as the processing unit, Amazon DynamoDB as the processing ledger, Amazon CloudWatch Logs for diagnostics, Amazon SQS for exhausted failures, and AWS IAM for the execution boundary. The implementation is deliberately narrow: four file extensions, one function, one table, one queue, and a manual deployment. The narrow scope makes it possible to examine each decision and each failure path in detail.

1.2 Motivation#

The project began with two practical questions. Could a file-processing pipeline be built and operated on AWS without a permanently running server? And could the resulting system be defended with evidence rather than assertions? The first question is an architecture exercise. The second is an engineering discipline exercise. A deployed function that appears to work in a console screenshot is not the same as a system whose validation order, idempotency rules, error taxonomy, and deployment package have been checked.

The work therefore treated the repository, the deployment, and the evidence as one artifact. Source code and tests describe intended behavior. Console captures and a captured SQS envelope describe what the deployed resources actually did. The case study keeps those sources separate and says which one supports each claim. This is slower than writing a feature list, but it produces a document that a reviewer can audit.

1.3 Purpose and objectives#

The project pursued six objectives:

  1. Build an event-driven pipeline in which an S3 upload automatically invokes Lambda and produces a durable processing record.
  2. Validate file type by extension, size, content signature, and decodability rather than trusting the file name.
  3. Extract useful metadata for supported image and text formats and compute a SHA-256 checksum over the original bytes.
  4. Make processing idempotent across duplicate S3 deliveries and safe under concurrent invocations.
  5. Separate permanent validation failures from transient infrastructure failures so that each follows the correct retry path.
  6. Deploy the system manually, document the steps, and collect evidence that distinguishes verified behavior from intended behavior.

1.4 Scope#

V1 covers a single AWS region and a single processing function. The supported inputs are .jpg, .jpeg, .png, and .txt. Extensions are case-insensitive. Files may be uploaded directly under incoming/ or under nested prefixes such as incoming/2026/photo.jpg or incoming/users/demo/file.txt. The S3 notification uses the incoming/ prefix and every s3:ObjectCreated:* event, with no suffix filter. Unsupported files therefore reach Lambda and are recorded as FAILED instead of being silently ignored.

The implemented resource set is Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon SQS, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and AWS IAM. Deployment is manual through the AWS Management Console, with AWS CLI commands for package upload and selected verification steps. There is no API Gateway, web frontend, Step Functions state machine, SNS topic, malware scanner, image resizer, or content-deduplication service. There is no infrastructure as code, CI/CD pipeline, or automated provisioning in V1. Those items are listed as future work, not as hidden features.

1.5 Intended users#

The document serves four audiences. A hiring manager or technical recruiter can read the executive summary, the highlights, and the results chapter to understand the scope and the evidence. A cloud or backend engineer can read the architecture, design, infrastructure, and testing chapters to evaluate the implementation. A reviewer can use the evidence inventory and the appendices to check specific claims. A future maintainer can use the configuration reference and the deployment commands to reproduce the environment.

1.6 The cost of manual and server-based processing#

Manual file handling does not scale because every upload depends on a person remembering the same sequence of checks. The checks drift, the results are not recorded consistently, and there is no reliable audit trail. A shared server improves consistency but introduces a new set of problems: the worker must be provisioned for peak load, patched for library and OS vulnerabilities, monitored for memory growth, and restarted after crashes. If the worker processes files sequentially, one bad input can block the queue. If it processes them in parallel, the database writes need concurrency control. Idle capacity is paid for even when no files arrive.

The event-driven model addresses the capacity and idle-cost problems, but it introduces at-least-once delivery and a harder failure boundary. S3 event notifications can be delivered more than once. Lambda asynchronous invocations can retry. A timeout or an unhandled exception can leave a record in an intermediate state. The design work moves from managing a server to managing identity, retries, state transitions, and evidence. SFPS treats those concerns as the core of the project.

1.7 Document conventions#

Chapters are numbered sequentially and use a decimal scheme for subsections. Figures and tables are numbered by chapter. Code excerpts are reproduced from the repository with minor whitespace adjustments for page width; they are not paraphrased. The AWS account identifier is written as <account-id> in prose and in the redacted SQS excerpt. The console screenshots show the project account identifier as part of resource names and ARNs; no access keys, secret keys, session tokens, or passwords appear in any capture.

The document uses the terms record, processing record, and item interchangeably for a DynamoDB item in the sfps-processing table. A validation failure means a permanent rejection of the input, such as an unsupported extension or corrupt image. An infrastructure failure means an AWS service error, an unexpected exception, or a configuration error that should be retried or investigated. A FAILED record is not the same thing as a failed Lambda invocation.

CHAPTER 2

Problem Statement and Requirements

2.1 Problem statement#

The system must accept files without a permanently running worker, decide whether each file is acceptable, extract metadata that is useful to a downstream consumer, and preserve a record of the outcome. The record must identify the exact S3 object version that was processed, including its version ID, rather than the object key alone. Duplicate notifications for the same version must not create a second logical result or overwrite a completed one. A bad file must fail in a way that is visible to an operator without causing an endless retry loop. A genuine infrastructure fault must be retried and, if it persists, must leave the original event somewhere an operator can inspect.

The problem has a security dimension as well. Uploaded files are untrusted input. The function must not execute them, must not trust their extensions, and must not write raw exception text or file contents into logs or the database. The bucket must remain private, encrypted, and reachable only over TLS. The execution role must be limited to the specific bucket prefix, table, queue, and log group used by the function.

2.2 Functional requirements#

The functional requirements below are derived from the PRD and checked against the implementation. The status column distinguishes requirements that are implemented and verified from those that are implemented but lack direct deployment evidence.

2.3 Nonfunctional requirements#

The nonfunctional requirements describe the qualities the system should have. Several are bounded by the V1 scope. For example, the function is designed to limit allocations before pixel decoding, but the deployed 512 MB memory boundary at the 25 MiB input ceiling has not been measured in this evidence set.

2.4 Supported formats and limits#

The 25 MiB ceiling is a hard cap. MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES may lower the limit but cannot raise it above 26,214,400 bytes. The image budget is calculated as width multiplied by height multiplied by the number of frames, and it is checked before pixel allocation. This matters for animated PNGs and for images that are small on disk but expensive to decode. Text statistics use regular-expression iterators so the function does not build per-word or per-line lists.

2.5 Error taxonomy#

The error codes are part of the public contract between the function, the DynamoDB record, and an operator reading the table. Validation codes identify inputs that will not become valid on retry. The infrastructure code identifies faults that may be transient. A malformed event is kept separate because no processing identity can be derived for it, so no record can be written.

2.6 Security expectations#

The bucket is private. Public access is blocked at the bucket level, a bucket policy denies requests that do not use TLS, and default encryption uses SSE-S3. The function reads only objects under the incoming/ prefix and uses GetObject and GetObjectVersion, which also authorize HeadObject. The execution role can read and write only the processing table, send only to the failure queue, and write only to the function's log group. The role cannot create log groups, so the log group is created before deployment.

Uploaded content is treated as hostile. The function never executes a file or trusts its extension. It checks the signature and decodes images with Pillow before accepting metadata. It decodes text strictly. Error messages persisted to DynamoDB come from a fixed allowlist. Unexpected exceptions are logged as sanitized stack frames without source lines, local variables, or raw exception text. The Lambda boundary raises a fixed-message InfrastructureError so SDK or decoder messages do not reach the runtime log or the destination responsePayload.

2.7 Operational constraints#

The deployment is manual in V1. Every resource is created in one AWS region, and the region must be used consistently in ARNs, policies, and the queue destination. The deployment archive must be built on Windows with Linux arm64 wheels and uploaded as a ZIP file under the 50 MB direct-upload limit. The function has a 30-second timeout and 512 MB of memory. The log group must exist before the first invocation because the execution role deliberately lacks logs:CreateLogGroup. S3 notification changes can take several minutes to become active, and bucket versioning has an initial propagation window before the first object operations.

These constraints are not defects. They are consequences of the chosen V1 scope and the least-privilege design. The deployment guide records them so that a future operator does not mistake a propagation delay or a missing log group for an application bug.

2.8 Requirements traceability and evidence status#

The PRD describes intended behavior. It is not, by itself, evidence that a requirement was implemented or tested. This case study uses three checks. The source code and tests establish what the repository implements. The console captures establish which resources exist and how they are configured. The deployed test fixtures and the SQS envelope establish what the deployed system did for a specific set of inputs. A requirement is marked verified only when the relevant check supports it.

The BUILD_STATE document dated 16 October 2026 recorded deployment acceptance as pending. The console captures and the SQS envelope are dated 18 October 2026, so they post-date that snapshot and confirm that a deployment and a test run occurred. They do not prove every item in the acceptance guide. In particular, the 25 MiB memory and timeout boundary, the exact attached IAM policy, the 30-day log retention value, and the per-file error codes in the truncated DynamoDB console view remain unverified or only partially verified. The evidence inventory records those gaps explicitly.

CHAPTER 3

Technology Stack

3.1 Selection principles#

The stack follows four principles. Use managed services for the undifferentiated parts of the pipeline: storage, compute invocation, state, queueing, logging, and identity. Keep the application code small enough to review in one sitting. Pin every runtime dependency so the deployed environment is deterministic. Choose tools that work on the available Windows development host without hiding the Linux target.

The result is a deliberately conventional AWS stack. There is no framework between the S3 event and the Python handler, no ORM over DynamoDB, and no container image. The function uses boto3 directly and Pillow for image validation. This makes the behavior visible in the source and keeps the deployment package understandable.

3.2 AWS services#

Amazon S3 stores the uploaded objects and emits the event that starts processing. Versioning is enabled because the processing identity depends on the version ID. The bucket is private, encrypted with SSE-S3, and protected by a TLS-only bucket policy. A lifecycle rule expires noncurrent versions after 30 days. S3 never receives a write from the function; the function only reads the pinned object version.

AWS Lambda runs the processing function. A single function handles all supported types and dispatches by validated extension. The runtime is Python 3.13 on arm64, with 512 MB of memory and a 30-second timeout. The function is invoked asynchronously by S3, which is why Lambda's retry count and on-failure destination apply. The handler is handler.lambda_handler, and the deployment package places handler.py at the archive root.

Amazon DynamoDB stores one processing record per S3 object version. The table uses on-demand capacity, a partition key named processing_id with type String, no sort key, no secondary indexes, and no point-in-time recovery in V1. Conditional writes provide the idempotency guarantee. The table is the operational ledger: an operator can see whether a version is PROCESSING, COMPLETED, or FAILED, and can read the metadata, checksum, or error map.

Amazon SQS receives asynchronous invocation failures that exhaust Lambda's function-error retries. The queue is a standard queue named sfps-failed-events, with 14-day message retention, a 30-second visibility timeout, SSE-SQS encryption, and no dead-letter queue. No consumer runs in V1. The queue exists so that a failed event is not lost when the function cannot complete it.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs stores the function's structured JSON application logs and the Lambda platform START, END, and REPORT lines. The log group is /aws/lambda/sfps-processor and is pre-created with 30-day retention. Application logs use one JSON object per line and include request_id, event_id, processing_id, bucket, object_key, version_id, file_type, file_size, status, processing_duration, and error fields where applicable.

AWS IAM defines the execution boundary. The role trusts lambda.amazonaws.com and carries a scoped inline policy. The policy allows s3:GetObject and s3:GetObjectVersion on the bucket's incoming/ prefix, dynamodb:GetItem, PutItem, and UpdateItem on the processing table, sqs:SendMessage on the failure queue, and logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents on the function's log group. There are no broad administrator permissions and no wildcard resources beyond the prefix and log-group suffixes required by the design.

3.3 Python and libraries#

Python 3.13 is used for local development, the Ruff target, and the Lambda runtime. The project standardized on one interpreter version to avoid a local-versus-deployed mismatch. The runtime dependency set is intentionally small: boto3 and botocore for AWS calls, jmespath and s3transfer as boto3 dependencies, Pillow for image validation and metadata, python-dateutil and six as transitive dependencies, and urllib3 as the HTTP layer. The standard library supplies hashlib, json, logging, os, time, datetime, io, re, warnings, and urllib.parse.

Pillow performs three jobs in the image path. It verifies the image structure, it reopens the same in-memory bytes and decodes every frame, and it reports the detected format and dimensions. The validation layer checks the signature before Pillow is called, checks the pixel budget before allocation, and maps expected decoder errors to CORRUPT_IMAGE. Unexpected errors such as MemoryError propagate to the infrastructure path instead of being mislabeled as a bad file.

Development tools are pytest for tests, moto for mocked S3 and DynamoDB, and Ruff for linting. The tests run offline with no AWS credentials or network access. The handler is reloaded inside a moto context so the boto3 clients created at import time are intercepted. The test fixtures build synthetic images and versioned S3 objects, which keeps the suite fast and deterministic.

3.4 Development and deployment tools#

Development runs on Windows 11 with PowerShell 5.1 and a Python 3.13 virtual environment. Dependencies are installed with pip from exact pins. The deployment package is assembled with pip's cross-platform wheel download, a flat copy of src/, and Python's zipfile module. The zip is verified for forward-slash entry names, a root-level handler.py, the presence of aarch64 extension modules, the absence of bytecode, and the 50 MB direct-upload limit. The AWS CLI uploads the archive and supports selected verification commands. The AWS Management Console is used for resource creation, inspection, and the acceptance walkthrough.

PowerShell 5.1 has two practical traps in this workflow. It does not support && or || command chaining, so the deployment commands use semicolons and explicit exit-code checks. Its Compress-Archive cmdlet writes backslash separators into ZIP entry names, which Lambda cannot unpack correctly. The project uses Python's zipfile with an explicit separator replacement and a verification assert instead.

3.5 Technology interactions#

3.6 Alternatives considered#

A long-running worker on EC2 or ECS was rejected for V1 because it would add capacity management and idle cost without improving the core demonstration. API Gateway and a web frontend were rejected because S3 already provides an event source and the project is about processing, not upload UX. AWS SAM, CloudFormation, and Terraform were deferred because the PRD explicitly requires a manual deployment that the owner can follow in the console. A KMS customer-managed key was deferred because SSE-S3 meets the stated encryption requirement without adding key-policy complexity. PDF and video processing were excluded because the validation and metadata rules would expand the scope substantially.

The architecture decision log records seventeen decisions, including the choice of exact pins, the manylinux_2_28_aarch64 platform tag, the failure classification, the strong duplicate read, and the decision to omit logs:CreateLogGroup. The most consequential decisions are summarized in Chapter 4 and revisited in Chapter 11.

CHAPTER 4

System Architecture

4.1 Architectural overview#

SFPS is a linear event-driven pipeline with one fan-out for diagnostics and one failure branch. An uploader writes an object under the incoming/ prefix of a private, versioned S3 bucket. S3 emits an ObjectCreated event with the bucket name, object key, size, version ID, and sequencer. The event asynchronously invokes the sfps-processor Lambda function. The function claims a processing record in DynamoDB, reads the object size with a version-pinned HeadObject, validates the extension and size, fetches the object bytes once with a version-pinned GetObject, validates the content, extracts metadata, computes SHA-256, and writes the terminal state. Application logs go to CloudWatch. If an infrastructure failure exhausts the asynchronous retry budget, Lambda sends an invocation envelope to the sfps-failed-events SQS queue.

The diagram is an original explanatory figure, not an AWS Console screenshot. The console capture in Figure 4.3 shows the same primary integration from the deployed function's point of view: S3 on the left as the trigger, the sfps-processor function in the center, and SQS on the right as the on-failure destination.

The pipeline is intentionally sequential within one invocation. A single S3 event can carry multiple records, and the handler processes them in order. A permanent validation failure is recorded and the loop continues. An infrastructure failure stops the batch and is re-raised. On retry, records that already reached COMPLETED are skipped, and the failing record is attempted again. Records later in the batch are not claimed until the failing record succeeds or becomes a permanent validation failure.

4.2 The event-driven workflow#

A single upload follows this sequence:

  1. The uploader writes the object to s3://sfps-incoming-<account-id>/incoming/... using the console or the AWS CLI.
  2. S3 stores the object as a new version and emits an ObjectCreated:* notification. The notification includes the bucket name, URL-encoded object key, object size, version ID, and sequencer.
  3. Lambda receives an asynchronous invocation. The handler parses the Records array and validates the bucket, key, and version ID types before deriving any identity.
  4. The handler computes processing_id from the canonical JSON encoding of bucket, object key, and version ID, then attempts a conditional PutItem with status PROCESSING.
  5. If the claim succeeds, the handler checks the incoming/ prefix, reads the authoritative size with HeadObject using the event version ID, rejects zero-byte and oversized objects, and validates the extension allowlist.
  6. For a supported type, the handler fetches the object once with GetObject using the same version ID, validates the content, extracts metadata, and computes SHA-256 over the bytes.
  7. The handler performs a conditional UpdateItem to COMPLETED, guarded so an existing COMPLETED record cannot be overwritten.
  8. The handler writes one JSON start line and one JSON terminal line to CloudWatch. A validation failure writes a FAILED record and returns successfully. An infrastructure failure logs sanitized diagnostics, attempts a guarded FAILED update, and re-raises.

4.3 Resource topology and trust boundaries#

The trust boundary is the AWS account and the region. The bucket, function, table, queue, and log group all live in ap-south-1. The function assumes an execution role through the Lambda service principal. The role's permissions are limited to the incoming/ prefix of the project bucket, the sfps-processing table, the sfps-failed-events queue, and the function's log group. The uploader is outside the processing boundary: it needs permission to write to the bucket, but the function never needs permission to write back to S3.

There are two data paths. The processing path carries object bytes from S3 to Lambda memory, then derived metadata and a checksum to DynamoDB. The diagnostic path carries log events from Lambda to CloudWatch. The failure path carries an invocation envelope from the Lambda asynchronous invocation system to SQS. The function does not send to SQS directly; the destination is configured on the function and is delivered by Lambda after retries are exhausted. This distinction matters when reading the envelope: requestPayload contains the entire original event, while requestContext describes the invocation, condition, and approximate invoke count.

4.4 Processing sequence#

Figure 4.2 shows the sequence for one object version. The first message is the asynchronous S3 event. The Lambda activation bar spans the rest of the processing. The function claims the DynamoDB record before reading S3, which means a claim failure can stop processing before any object bytes are fetched. The size check is a HeadObject, not a download. The content read is a single GetObject. Validation, decoding, and hashing happen in memory on that one byte sequence. The terminal write is the only state transition after the claim.

The diagram omits the internal branch where a duplicate COMPLETED record is skipped before any S3 call. That path returns from the claim step, logs a duplicate message, and performs no HeadObject or GetObject. It is described in Chapter 5 with the conditional write protocol.

4.5 Object versioning and version-pinned reads#

Versioning is not a background convenience in SFPS. It is part of the processing identity. When an object is overwritten, S3 creates a new version ID. The event for the new upload carries the new version ID, so the function treats it as a separate processing identity and writes a separate record. The old version remains addressable until the lifecycle rule expires it. This is why the DynamoDB scan in Chapter 9 contains two sample.png records with different sizes and outcomes: they are two versions of the same key, not a duplicate write.

Every read uses the version ID from the event. HeadObject is called with VersionId, so the authoritative size belongs to the exact version that triggered the event. GetObject is called with the same VersionId, so the bytes that are validated, hashed, and measured are the bytes identified by the record. There is no fallback to the latest version. If the version ID is missing, empty, or the string null, the record is malformed and the handler raises before writing an identity. A latest-version fallback would make the record describe a different object than the event, which is worse than failing loudly.

The lifecycle rule permanently deletes noncurrent versions after 30 days. This bounds storage growth from repeated uploads while keeping recent versions available for investigation. It does not affect current versions and it does not change the processing identity of a new upload.

4.6 Nested prefixes#

The trigger prefix is incoming/, not a flat folder. S3 keys are strings, so incoming/2026/photo.jpg and incoming/users/demo/file.txt are valid keys under the same prefix. The handler checks that the decoded key starts with incoming/, extracts the file name from the last path segment, and derives the extension from that segment. Dots in directory names are irrelevant. The positive test suite includes a nested/ folder and a completed 06-nested-image.jpg record, which shows that the deployed path handling works beyond a single-level upload.

4.7 Failure classification#

The failure model is the most important design decision in the project. A validation failure means the input is permanently unacceptable. The function records FAILED with a fixed error code, logs the outcome, returns successfully, and continues with the next record. Retrying the same bytes would produce the same result, so a retry would only waste invocations and delay the queue. An infrastructure failure means the function could not complete the work because of an AWS service error, an unexpected exception, or a configuration problem. The function logs sanitized diagnostics, attempts a guarded FAILED update when a record exists, and re-raises. Lambda then applies its asynchronous retry policy, and the event can reach SQS.

A mixed batch complicates the story. If one record fails permanently and a later record fails with an infrastructure error, the entire original event is retried and can be delivered to SQS. The destination envelope then contains every original record, including the permanent failure that did not itself request a retry. This is a property of Lambda's asynchronous invocation model, not a bug in the classification. The PRD and the README both call it out.

4.8 Asynchronous retries and the failure destination#

S3 invokes Lambda asynchronously. The function's asynchronous invocation configuration sets MaximumRetryAttempts to 2, which allows the initial attempt plus up to two function-error retries. Throttling and Lambda system errors use separate retry behavior up to the maximum event age, which is left at the default of six hours. Duplicate delivery remains possible. The on-failure destination is configured as an SQS destination with condition On failure, not as a classic dead-letter queue.

The captured SQS message in Chapter 9 confirms the envelope shape for one injected failure. requestContext.condition is RetriesExhausted, approximateInvokeCount is 3, requestPayload contains the original S3 event for incoming/images.jpg, and responsePayload contains a sanitized InfrastructureError with the fixed message and a stack trace that stops at the handler boundary. That is the expected destination behavior. It does not prove that every possible failure mode produces the same envelope, and it does not prove that the retry timing matches a particular schedule.

4.9 Observability#

CloudWatch receives two kinds of log lines. The Lambda platform writes START, END, and REPORT lines for each invocation. The application writes one JSON object per line through the sfps logger. A successful record produces a PROCESSING start line and a COMPLETED terminal line. A permanent failure produces a PROCESSING line and a FAILED terminal line. A duplicate skip produces an explicit duplicate message. An infrastructure failure produces a diagnostic line with sanitized stack frames and then the boundary exception. The application logger sets propagate to False, so the same record is not duplicated through the runtime root logger.

The log group is pre-created with 30-day retention. The execution role can create log streams and put log events but cannot create the log group, which is why the group must exist before the first invocation. The captured log group page shows the group and its Standard log class; the retention value is not visible in that capture, so the 30-day setting is documented rather than visually verified.

4.10 Architecture status and evidence#

The architecture is implemented and deployed. The console captures show the S3 trigger, the Lambda function, the DynamoDB table, the CloudWatch log group, the IAM role page, and the SQS destination. The SQS envelope shows a real exhausted failure. The parts that remain unverified are configuration details that the captures do not expose, such as the exact attached IAM policy, the bucket policy text, the lifecycle rule, and the log retention value. Those are documented in the repository and the deployment guide, and they are listed in the evidence inventory rather than presented as visual proof.

CHAPTER 5

Application Design and Processing Logic

5.1 Source organization#

The repository separates AWS orchestration from pure file logic. handler.py owns event parsing, AWS calls, the conditional write protocol, error categorization, configuration, and logging. validation.py owns extension, signature, image, and text validation. checksum.py owns the SHA-256 helper. processors/image.py and processors/text.py own metadata extraction. The pure modules never import boto3, so they can be tested without mocks. The handler tests use moto to intercept S3 and DynamoDB and invoke the handler with synthetic S3 events.

5.2 Configuration contract#

The function reads three environment variables at import time. TABLE_NAME is required and must be non-empty. MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES is optional and defaults to 26,214,400 bytes; it must parse as an integer from 1 through 26,214,400. LOG_LEVEL is optional and defaults to INFO; it must be a valid Python logging level name. Invalid configuration raises ConfigurationError at import, which is intentionally loud. The error message does not echo the raw value or a chained parsing exception.

5.3 Handler lifecycle#

The module loads configuration and creates one boto3 S3 client and one DynamoDB Table handle at import time. Lambda reuses the execution environment across invocations, so the clients are created once per cold start and reused. The logger is configured once, with a JSON formatter, propagate set to False, and handlers cleared before a new one is attached so module reloads remain idempotent under pytest. The handler entry point parses the Records array, loops over the records sequentially, and wraps the loop in a boundary that converts unexpected exceptions into a fixed-message InfrastructureError.

5.4 Event parsing and processing identity#

The handler accepts only an event with a non-empty Records array. Each record must be an object with an s3 section, a bucket name, an object key, and a version ID. Bucket, key, and version must be non-empty strings; the version cannot be whitespace-only or the literal string null. The optional sequencer must be a string when present. The key is decoded with unquote_plus, so %XX escapes and plus signs decode correctly. A malformed record raises MalformedEventError before any identity is derived or any AWS write is attempted.

The processing identity is a SHA-256 digest of canonical JSON containing the bucket, object key, and version ID. Canonical JSON uses sorted keys and compact separators, which makes the encoding injective for arbitrary key strings. Naive concatenation would be ambiguous if keys contained the delimiter. The result is a fixed 64-character hexadecimal string used as the DynamoDB partition key.

The file name is the last path segment of the decoded key. The file type is the lowercased extension without the dot, or absent when the file name has no extension. The extension parser uses rpartition on the last segment, so dots in directory names do not confuse it. A trailing dot with no characters after it returns no extension.

5.5 Validation workflow#

Validation is ordered to avoid unnecessary work and to make the error code unambiguous. The prefix check runs first because a key outside incoming/ cannot be a legitimate event for this pipeline. The size check runs before the extension check so a zero-byte folder marker is reported as ZERO_BYTE rather than UNSUPPORTED_EXTENSION. The extension check runs before any content download, so an unsupported PDF is rejected without reading its 1.6 MB body. Content validation runs after the single GetObject.

5.6 Image validation and metadata#

Image validation does not rely on Pillow alone. The handler first checks the extension against the allowlist, then the bytes against the claimed signature: FF D8 FF for JPEG and 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A for PNG. A mismatch is TYPE_MISMATCH before any decoder work. If the signature matches, the validator opens the image, checks the total pixel budget, calls verify, closes the image, reopens the same in-memory bytes, checks the budget again, and decodes every frame. The detected format must match the extension. Expected malformed-image errors become CORRUPT_IMAGE. Decompression-bomb warnings and errors become IMAGE_DIMENSIONS_EXCEEDED. Unexpected errors such as MemoryError propagate to the infrastructure path.

The metadata processor reopens the validated bytes to read width, height, and image.format. It checks the budget again and returns a dictionary with exactly those three keys. The reopen is an in-memory decode, not another S3 download. The single-read requirement refers to one version-pinned GetObject, not to one Pillow open.

5.7 Text validation and metadata#

Text validation decodes the bytes as strict UTF-8. Invalid sequences become INVALID_ENCODING. A single leading byte-order mark (U+FEFF) is removed after decoding. A BOM-only payload becomes an empty string at this layer; a truly zero-byte object is rejected earlier by the size check. The text processor counts Unicode code points for characters, whitespace-separated runs for words, and splitlines-style boundaries for lines. A trailing newline does not create an extra line. Whitespace-only text is valid and may contain zero words.

The counters use regular-expression iterators rather than split or splitlines lists. A 200,000-line stress test in the regression suite confirms that the extra allocation stays below 1 MiB. This is a deliberate resource-bound decision: a 25 MiB text file with millions of short words should not create a list proportional to the word count.

5.8 SHA-256#

The checksum is computed over the original bytes returned by the version-pinned GetObject. It is not computed over re-encoded image data, decoded text, or metadata. This makes the stored digest a fingerprint of the uploaded object version. The checksum is metadata in V1; the system does not use it for content-level deduplication. A known-digest test anchors the helper to the standard SHA-256 values for empty bytes and for the string abc.

5.9 DynamoDB record schema#

Every processing record has the same identity fields and one of three statuses. The terminal transition adds file_size and processed_at. A COMPLETED record adds sha256, metadata, and file_type, and removes any stale error. A FAILED record adds an error map and, when known, file_size and file_type. The error map has exactly error_code, error_type, and message. Its serialized size stays within 1,024 characters; only the message is truncated if necessary.

5.10 Processing states#

A record begins in PROCESSING when the claim PutItem succeeds. It ends in COMPLETED after a successful validation, metadata extraction, checksum, and terminal update, or in FAILED after a permanent validation failure or an infrastructure failure that has a record to update. A PROCESSING record can be re-attempted by a later delivery. A FAILED record can also be re-attempted. A COMPLETED record is never re-attempted. The terminal update is guarded, so a late duplicate cannot overwrite a completed result.

5.11 Conditional writes and idempotency#

The write protocol has two conditional operations. The claim is a PutItem conditioned on attribute_not_exists(processing_id). If the condition fails, the handler reads the existing item with ConsistentRead=True. If the existing status is COMPLETED, the handler logs a duplicate and returns without touching S3. If the status is PROCESSING or FAILED, the handler continues the re-attempt without overwriting created_at. The terminal operation is an UpdateItem conditioned on attribute_exists(processing_id) AND status <> COMPLETED. A terminal conditional failure means another invocation already completed the record; it is logged and treated as already satisfied.

The consistent read matters. An eventually consistent read could return a stale PROCESSING item for a version that another invocation has just completed, and the handler would reprocess it. ConsistentRead closes that window. The regression suite includes a simulated stale replica that would have triggered an S3 fetch; the handler must not fetch S3 in that case.

5.12 Failure classification and sanitized logging#

The handler catches ValidationError separately from every other exception. A validation error writes FAILED through the guarded terminal update, logs a terminal FAILED line, and returns. If the FAILED write itself fails, the handler logs a secondary failure and re-raises so the batch can retry. Any other exception is logged with a diagnostic line that includes sanitized stack frames, then a guarded FAILED write is attempted when the record exists, and the exception is re-raised. At the outer Lambda boundary, the handler raises a fixed-message InfrastructureError from None, so raw SDK or decoder text does not escape through the runtime log or the destination responsePayload.

The JSON formatter keeps diagnostic frame filenames, function names, and line numbers, and omits exception text, chained exception text, source lines, and local variable values. The persisted message is chosen from an allowlist before the 1,024-character cap is applied. The cap truncates only the message field; error_code and error_type are never truncated. The application logger does not propagate to the runtime root logger, which prevents a second unstructured copy of each record.

5.13 Design limits and deliberate omissions#

The handler does not write to S3, move objects, delete objects, or resize images. It does not scan for malware. It does not deduplicate content by SHA-256. It does not use a DynamoDB transaction across multiple records. It does not implement a retry loop inside the function; retries are delegated to Lambda's asynchronous invocation behavior. Each omission is a scope decision, not an accident. The V1 design favors a small, auditable processing path over a larger feature set that would be harder to verify.

CHAPTER 6

AWS Infrastructure Implementation

6.1 Deployment model#

V1 is deployed manually in a single region. The project owner creates each resource in the AWS Management Console, using AWS CLI commands for package upload and selected verification steps. The deployment guide in the repository lists every console path, policy document, and acceptance step. The captures in this chapter show the resources that were created and the values that are visible in the console.

The region used in the captured deployment is ap-south-1 (Asia Pacific, Mumbai). Every ARN, queue URL, and policy resource in the deployment must use that region. The account identifier is written as <account-id> in this document. The bucket name is sfps-incoming-<account-id> in the documentation; the captures show the deployed name with the account number.

6.2 Amazon S3 bucket and configuration#

The bucket is a general-purpose bucket with Block all public access enabled, versioning enabled, and default encryption set to SSE-S3. A bucket policy denies every request whose aws:SecureTransport condition is false, which enforces TLS. A lifecycle rule named expire-noncurrent-30d permanently deletes noncurrent versions after 30 days. The S3 event notification is configured on the Lambda side with the incoming/ prefix and all object-created events.

Figure 6.1 establishes the bucket name and the top-level prefix. Figure 6.2 opens the prefix and shows the acceptance files. The sizes and names are consistent with the DynamoDB records later in the document: sample.jpg is 137.8 KB, sample.png is part of the image set, sample.pdf is 1.6 MB, and images.jpg is 44.1 KB. The partially visible row at the top of the folder is the nested sample.txt upload described in the acceptance walkthrough.

The captured S3 pages do not show the Properties or Permissions tabs, so they do not visually prove versioning, encryption, public-access blocking, the TLS policy, or the lifecycle rule. Those settings are documented in the README and the console guide and are treated as implemented configuration, not as visual evidence. The bucket and prefix structure is visually verified.

6.3 Amazon DynamoDB table#

The sfps-processing table uses processing_id as a String partition key, no sort key, on-demand capacity, AWS-owned encryption, and no point-in-time recovery. There are no secondary indexes. The table is the operational ledger for the pipeline. Figure 6.3 shows the table browser with the Scan view selected and all attributes projected.

On-demand capacity was chosen because the workload is bursty and the project has no traffic forecast. The table does not use a sort key because the processing identity is already unique per object version. The absence of PITR and secondary indexes is a V1 scope decision. It keeps the table simple and avoids extra cost, but it also means there is no historical recovery or alternate query path beyond a scan. Chapter 13 treats that as a limitation.

6.4 Amazon SQS failure queue#

The sfps-failed-events queue is a standard queue with SSE-SQS encryption, a 14-day message retention period, a 30-second visibility timeout, and no dead-letter queue. No consumer runs in V1. The queue is configured as the Lambda function's on-failure destination, not as a classic DLQ. The execution role has sqs:SendMessage on the queue ARN, which the destination delivery requires.

The queue is intentionally not the primary error path for invalid files. A PDF upload or a corrupt image becomes a FAILED DynamoDB record and does not reach SQS. The queue is for events that could not be processed because of an infrastructure fault after retries. This separation keeps the queue signal meaningful: a message in sfps-failed-events means an operational fault, not an ordinary rejected upload.

6.5 IAM role and scoped policy#

The execution role trusts lambda.amazonaws.com. The documented role name is sfps-lambda-role, with an inline policy named sfps-lambda-scoped-policy. The captured IAM page shows a role named sfps-lambda-scoped-policy, created on 18 October 2026, with a one-hour maximum session duration. The role page does not show the attached policy document. The policy below is the repository-documented policy and should be treated as the intended configuration, not as a transcription of the console capture.

The policy deliberately omits logs:CreateLogGroup. That forces the operator to pre-create the log group, which is a small deployment step and a meaningful least-privilege choice. It also omits s3:ListBucket, DynamoDB scan or delete actions, and any wildcard resource outside the prefix and log-group suffixes required by the design. The role cannot read objects outside incoming/, cannot write to another table, and cannot send to another queue.

6.6 Lambda function configuration#

The function is named sfps-processor, uses the Python 3.13 runtime, runs on arm64, has 512 MB of memory, and has a 30-second timeout. The package type is Zip. The handler is handler.lambda_handler. The function has no layers. The captured function list shows the runtime and package type; the general configuration page shows the memory and timeout.

The 512 MB memory setting is also the CPU allocation lever in Lambda. A higher memory setting can reduce duration for CPU-bound work, but it also raises the per-millisecond cost. The project chose 512 MB as a balance between image decoding needs and cost, without claiming that it is optimal. The 30-second timeout is well above the observed successful invocation durations, but the boundary input at 25 MiB was not measured on the deployed function.

6.7 Environment variables#

The deployed environment has three variables: TABLE_NAME set to sfps-processing, MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES set to 26214400, and LOG_LEVEL set to INFO. The explicit values match the documented defaults and make the deployed configuration visible without reading code. The function validates the values at import and fails loudly if they are wrong.

6.8 Asynchronous invocation and the SQS destination#

The asynchronous invocation configuration sets MaximumRetryAttempts to 2 and leaves the maximum event age at the default six hours. The destination is an SQS destination with condition On failure and destination ARN arn:aws:sqs:ap-south-1:<account-id>:sfps-failed-events. Figure 8.2 in the security chapter shows the destination page. The function overview in Figure 4.3 shows the same integration from the function's diagram view.

The destination is not a classic dead-letter queue. Lambda sends an invocation envelope with requestContext, requestPayload, and responseContext/responsePayload. requestPayload contains the entire original S3 event. The responsePayload of an exhausted invocation is sanitized by the handler boundary, which raises a fixed-message InfrastructureError from None. The captured envelope in Chapter 9 confirms that behavior.

6.9 S3 event trigger and invoke permission#

The S3 trigger is configured with event types s3:ObjectCreated:*, prefix incoming/, and an empty suffix. The trigger details show the bucket ARN, the notification name, the service principal s3.amazonaws.com, the source account, and the statement ID. Creating the trigger from the Lambda console creates both the bucket notification and the resource-based invoke permission. The permission is scoped by source ARN and source account.

The empty suffix is important. A suffix filter for .jpg or .txt would prevent unsupported files from reaching Lambda, and the system would have no explicit record that they were rejected. With no suffix filter, a PDF or CSV reaches the function, fails validation, and produces a FAILED record. The queue remains reserved for infrastructure faults.

6.10 CloudWatch log group and retention#

The log group is /aws/lambda/sfps-processor. It is pre-created because the execution role cannot create it. The documented retention is 30 days. The captured log group page shows the group and its Standard log class; the retention column is not visible in the capture. The function writes one JSON object per line, and the Lambda platform writes its own START, END, and REPORT lines. Figure 6.9 shows seven recent log streams, which is consistent with several execution environments over the test window.

6.11 Deployment evidence status#

The console captures confirm that the bucket, prefix structure, DynamoDB table, Lambda function, environment variables, trigger, log group, IAM role page, and SQS destination exist. They do not confirm every configuration value. The evidence inventory in the appendix marks each item as visually verified, documented, or missing. This distinction is deliberate. A professional case study should not turn a console page that happens to be open into proof of a setting that is on another tab.

CHAPTER 7

Deployment and Packaging

7.1 Windows development environment#

The repository is developed on Windows 11 with PowerShell 5.1 and Python 3.13.14. The Lambda target is Linux arm64. Those two facts create the main packaging problem: the build host cannot install the target's native wheels with a normal pip install, because pip would resolve wheels for the host platform. The project solves this with pip's cross-platform options: --python-version 3.13, --implementation cp, --abi cp313, --platform manylinux_2_28_aarch64, --only-binary=:all:, and --no-compile.

The virtual environment is created with python -m venv .venv and activated with .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1. If PowerShell execution policy blocks activation, the same commands can be run with the explicit interpreter path .venv\Scripts\python.exe. The build does not depend on a globally installed Python package set.

7.2 Dependencies and the requirements lock#

requirements.txt pins all eight runtime packages: boto3 1.43.112, botocore 1.43.112, jmespath 1.1.0, Pillow 12.3.0, python-dateutil 2.9.0.post0, s3transfer 0.19.2, six 1.17.0, and urllib3 2.8.0. requirements-dev.txt includes the runtime file and pins pytest 9.1.1, moto 5.2.4, and Ruff 0.17.0. Pinning every runtime transitive matters because the Lambda runtime also ships boto3; the project bundles its own pinned SDK so the deployed version does not drift with the runtime.

The build record found a previous package with botocore 1.43.113 while local tests used 1.43.112. That mismatch is exactly the kind of drift the lock is meant to prevent. The verified archive for this case study contains botocore 1.43.112 in its metadata, matching requirements.txt. The older workspace build/ directory still contains 1.43.113; it is a stale artifact and is not the archive used for deployment.

7.3 Why Windows-native binaries cannot be uploaded#

A Python wheel is not always pure Python. Pillow ships compiled extension modules for image decoding, color management, fonts, and format support. On Windows those modules are .pyd files built for the Windows ABI. On Linux arm64 they are .so files built for the Linux ABI and the target CPU architecture. A Lambda function running on Linux arm64 cannot load a Windows .pyd file, and it cannot load an x86-64 .so file. The import would fail before the handler ran.

The same rule applies to any dependency with native code. Pure-Python packages can be packaged from any host, but binary packages must match the target's operating system, CPU architecture, Python ABI, and C library. The build command tells pip to download the target wheels instead of the host wheels, even though the download runs on Windows.

7.4 The manylinux_2_28_aarch64 platform tag#

Lambda's Python 3.13 runtime runs on Amazon Linux 2023, which provides glibc 2.34. The manylinux_2_28 tag requires glibc 2.28 or newer, so it is compatible with the runtime. The PRD originally used manylinux2014_aarch64, which requires an older baseline. Pillow 12.3.0 does not publish a manylinux2014 aarch64 wheel for cp313; pip resolution for that tag stops at Pillow 12.2.0. Rather than downgrade Pillow or relax the lock, the project moved the build to manylinux_2_28_aarch64, which has a cp313 aarch64 wheel for the pinned version.

The --no-compile flag prevents pip from writing __pycache__ and .pyc files during the target install. The build also sweeps src/ for __pycache__ before copying. The archive verification checks that no bytecode or dev artifact is present. The older build/ directory is not used as evidence because it contains an older botocore version; the verified function.zip is the release artifact.

7.5 ZIP package layout#

Lambda expects the handler module at the path named by the handler setting. The function is configured as handler.lambda_handler, so handler.py must sit at the ZIP root, not inside a src/ folder. The build copies the contents of src/ into build/, then zips the contents of build/ rather than the build/ directory itself. The ZIP entry names must use forward slashes. PowerShell 5.1's Compress-Archive writes backslash separators, which Lambda cannot unpack correctly, so the project uses Python's zipfile with os.sep replaced by a forward slash.

The command in Code 7.1 is a readable line-wrapped form of the repository command. In PowerShell, the backtick is the line-continuation character, and the Python zipfile expression must remain on the logical line passed to python -c. The repository README contains the exact single-line commands used for the build.

7.6 Package verification results#

The verification was repeated for this case study by inspecting the existing function.zip. The archive is below the 50 MB direct-upload limit, so no S3-hosted upload was necessary. The presence of aarch64 .so files is strong evidence that the package contains Linux arm64 binaries rather than Windows binaries. It is not proof that every native extension imports correctly at runtime; the deployed invocations provide that evidence for the code paths they exercised.

7.7 Upload and runtime configuration#

The package is uploaded through the Lambda console (Code, Upload from, .zip file) or with the AWS CLI: aws lambda update-function-code --function-name sfps-processor --zip-file fileb://function.zip --region ap-south-1. After upload, the handler is set to handler.lambda_handler, the runtime to Python 3.13, the architecture to arm64, the memory to 512 MB, and the timeout to 30 seconds. The environment variables are set as shown in Chapter 6. The asynchronous invocation configuration and the SQS destination are configured separately.

The deployment guide recommends verifying the last update status before testing. It also warns that the package is larger than the embedded editor's 3 MB threshold, so the source tree may not be visible in the console even when the upload succeeded. That warning prevents a false diagnosis: an empty editor is not evidence that the package failed to upload.

7.8 Deployment challenges and solutions#

The first packaging attempt used the PRD's original manylinux2014_aarch64 platform tag. Pip could not resolve Pillow 12.3.0 for cp313 under that tag; it offered at most 12.2.0. The project could have downgraded Pillow, but the dependency pins were treated as fixed. The resolution was to change the platform tag to manylinux_2_28_aarch64 and document the reason in ADR-012. This is a useful example of a build constraint that is invisible until the exact combination of Python version, library version, and platform tag is tested.

The second challenge was bytecode in the package. Pip's --target install byte-compiles by default, which produced __pycache__ and .pyc files that violated the package's no-bytecode check. The --no-compile flag prevents the problem at the source, and a __pycache__ sweep remains as a guard. The third challenge was ZIP entry separators. Compress-Archive produced backslash names that Lambda could not unpack. The Python zipfile command with an explicit separator replacement fixed it, and the verification assert catches a regression before upload.

A fourth challenge is evidence drift. The workspace build/ directory contains an older botocore 1.43.113, while the release archive contains 1.43.112. A casual inspection of build/ would therefore describe the wrong package. The project treats function.zip as the release artifact and compares its installed metadata against requirements.txt. The stale build directory is left in place but is not cited as evidence. This is a small example of a larger lesson: a build directory is not a release record.

CHAPTER 8

Security and Reliability

8.1 Security model and boundaries#

SFPS treats the uploaded file as untrusted input and the AWS account as the trust boundary. The bucket is private, the function has a narrow execution role, and the object content never leaves the AWS services that need it. The function reads bytes into memory, validates them without executing them, and writes only derived metadata, a checksum, and a small error map to DynamoDB. It does not write files to disk, spawn subprocesses, or call external services.

The security review looks at four surfaces: the storage boundary, the compute boundary, the identity boundary, and the diagnostic boundary. The storage boundary covers public access, TLS, encryption, and versioning. The compute boundary covers input validation, resource limits, and the absence of code execution. The identity boundary covers IAM scope and resource-level restrictions. The diagnostic boundary covers log fields, error messages, and destination payloads.

8.2 Private S3 access and TLS#

Block all public access is enabled on the bucket. The bucket policy denies every s3:* request whose aws:SecureTransport condition is false. This is a deny-only policy with Principal "*"; it does not grant public access. The console may warn about the wildcard principal, but the statement only denies non-TLS requests. The function's IAM policy grants read access only to the incoming/ prefix, so even a compromised function could not read objects elsewhere in the bucket.

The project does not use presigned URLs, a public website endpoint, or an S3 static website configuration. Uploads are performed by an authenticated principal through the console or the AWS CLI over TLS. The function never writes to S3, so there is no write path to protect beyond the uploader's own permissions.

8.3 Encryption#

Default encryption is SSE-S3, which encrypts each object at rest with Amazon S3 managed keys. S3 Bucket Keys apply to SSE-KMS, not SSE-S3, so there is no bucket-key setting to configure for this design. The SQS queue uses SSE-SQS by default. DynamoDB uses AWS-owned encryption. These choices meet the V1 requirement to encrypt data at rest without adding a customer-managed KMS key and its key-policy surface. A KMS customer-managed key is a reasonable future enhancement for organizations that need key rotation control or cross-account key policies.

8.4 IAM least privilege#

The execution role trusts only lambda.amazonaws.com. The inline policy grants four groups of actions. S3 read access is limited to the bucket's incoming/ prefix. DynamoDB access is limited to GetItem, PutItem, and UpdateItem on the processing table. SQS access is limited to SendMessage on the failure queue. CloudWatch access is limited to CreateLogStream and PutLogEvents on the function's log group. There is no s3:ListBucket, no DynamoDB Scan, no DeleteItem, and no wildcard resource outside the required prefix and log-group suffix.

The role deliberately lacks logs:CreateLogGroup, which is why the log group is pre-created. This is a small operational inconvenience and a meaningful reduction in scope. The role cannot create new log groups, change retention, or delete logs. It can only write to the group that the deployment created.

The captured role page is named sfps-lambda-scoped-policy, while the repository documentation uses sfps-lambda-role for the role and sfps-lambda-scoped-policy for the inline policy. The difference is recorded here rather than smoothed over. The page confirms that a role with the policy name exists and was created on 18 October 2026. It does not show the attached policy document, so the action-level scope is verified from the repository policy and the deployment guide, not from this capture.

8.5 Resource-scoped permissions#

Resource scoping is the part of least privilege that is easiest to get wrong. The S3 statement uses arn:aws:s3:::sfps-incoming-<account-id>/incoming/*, not the bucket ARN alone. The DynamoDB statement uses the table ARN, not a wildcard table pattern. The SQS statement uses the queue ARN. The CloudWatch statement uses the log-group ARN with the :* suffix required for log streams. These are deliberately scoped wildcards, not broad grants. The deployment guide explicitly tells the operator not to add s3:ListBucket, DynamoDB scan/delete, or administrator policies to the execution role.

The Lambda resource-based policy is a separate boundary. It allows s3.amazonaws.com to invoke the function, scoped by AWS:SourceArn to the bucket and AWS:SourceAccount to the account. The trigger details in Figure 6.7 show the service principal and source account. If an older console creates the statement without the source conditions, the guide provides CLI commands to remove and re-add it with the restriction.

8.6 Version-pinned processing#

Version pinning is a reliability control as well as a correctness control. If an object is overwritten while an event is being processed, an unpinned read could fetch the new bytes while the record still refers to the old event. SFPS passes the event's version ID to both HeadObject and GetObject, so the size and bytes belong to the same version. A missing or null version ID is a malformed event, not a cue to read the latest version. This avoids a silent mismatch between the recorded identity and the processed content.

The lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 30 days bounds storage growth. It does not remove the current version. A version that is still current remains readable even after its record is completed. If an operator needs to investigate an old event after the noncurrent window, the bytes may no longer exist, but the DynamoDB record and the CloudWatch logs remain. That is a deliberate retention trade-off, not an oversight.

8.7 DynamoDB state tracking and conditional writes#

The table records PROCESSING, COMPLETED, and FAILED states. The claim is conditional, so two concurrent invocations cannot both create the same processing_id. The terminal update is conditional on status <> COMPLETED, so a late or duplicate invocation cannot overwrite a completed result. The duplicate path uses ConsistentRead=True after a claim conflict, which prevents a stale replica from causing unnecessary reprocessing. These controls are tested with duplicate delivery, a PROCESSING re-attempt, and a simulated terminal race.

The table does not use transactions across records. Each record is independent, which matches the per-version processing model. A mixed batch can leave earlier records COMPLETED while a later record fails. That is expected. The batch is not a unit of atomicity; the object version is.

8.8 Retry and failure destination#

Lambda asynchronous invocation retries function errors up to two times after the initial attempt. Throttling and system errors have separate retry behavior up to the maximum event age. The on-failure destination is SQS, not a classic DLQ. The execution role needs sqs:SendMessage on the queue for the destination to work. The queue has no consumer in V1, so a message stays until the 14-day retention period expires unless an operator deletes it.

A permanent validation failure does not itself trigger retries or destination delivery. A mixed batch can still be retried and delivered if another record in the same event fails with an infrastructure error. The destination envelope then contains every original record. This behavior is documented in the PRD, the README, and the deployment guide because it is easy to misread as a failed validation sending itself to SQS.

8.9 Structured logs and sanitized diagnostics#

The application logger writes one JSON object per line. The formatter includes a fixed set of fields and omits absent values. Stack traces include frame filenames, function names, and line numbers, and omit exception text, chained causes, source lines, and local variables. Persisted error messages come from an allowlist, and unexpected exceptions become a fixed infrastructure message. The outer Lambda boundary raises a fixed-message InfrastructureError from None, so raw SDK or decoder text does not appear in the runtime log or the destination responsePayload.

The regression suite exercises these surfaces with a marker string that must not appear in the persisted error, the emitted JSON, or the rendered uncaught exception. The test includes a chained cause, because exception chaining is a common leak path. The logger's propagate flag is False, and a test installs a root handler to confirm that application records do not reach it.

8.10 Duplicate event handling#

S3 event notifications are at-least-once. Duplicate delivery of the same bucket, key, and version is possible. The handler skips only COMPLETED records. A PROCESSING record is re-attempted, because the previous attempt may have crashed before the terminal write. A FAILED record is re-attempted, because a later delivery may succeed after a transient fault. The created_at timestamp is never overwritten. The terminal update cannot overwrite COMPLETED. Together these rules make retries converge to the true terminal state.

The duplicate path performs no S3 fetch when the record is already COMPLETED. A regression test simulates a stale read and a forbidden HeadObject call, so a future change that reintroduces the fetch fails the test. This matters for cost and latency as well as correctness: duplicate notifications should not re-download objects.

8.11 Data retention#

S3 noncurrent versions expire after 30 days. CloudWatch log retention is 30 days. SQS messages are retained for 14 days. DynamoDB records have no TTL and remain until deleted. The error map is capped at 1,024 serialized characters. The function does not store file contents in DynamoDB or CloudWatch. The only copy of the original bytes is the S3 object version.

The asymmetry is intentional. Processing records are the operational ledger and are kept for inspection. Source objects are retained as current versions and for 30 days as noncurrent versions. Logs and failure messages have shorter windows because they are diagnostic, not the system of record. A future retention policy could add a DynamoDB TTL or an archive export, but V1 does not.

8.12 Reliability limitations and operational risks#

The design has real limitations. There is no automated alarm when a message lands in SQS. There is no consumer that replays failed events. There is no dead-letter queue for the SQS queue itself. There is no cross-region replication. The DynamoDB table has no point-in-time recovery. The function has no reserved concurrency, so a sudden burst can be throttled. The 25 MiB memory and timeout boundary has not been measured on the deployed function. The IAM policy attachment is documented but not visually verified. The log retention value is documented but not visible in the capture.

These are not reasons to call the system unreliable for its V1 purpose. They are reasons not to call it production-grade without additional work. A production deployment would add alarms, a replay procedure, load and boundary tests, a recovery plan, and probably infrastructure as code. Chapter 13 lists those enhancements and separates them from what exists today.

8.13 Claims not made#

The project does not claim that the bucket configuration is production-grade for regulated data, that the IAM policy has been penetration-tested, that the function is immune to decoder vulnerabilities, or that the queue is monitored. It does not claim multi-region durability, zero data loss, or a recovery point objective. It does not claim that the deployed function has been load-tested. The security and reliability claims are limited to the controls that are implemented and the evidence that is shown.

CHAPTER 9

Testing Strategy and Test Execution

9.1 Testing approach#

The testing strategy uses three layers. The first layer is a pure unit suite for validation, checksum, image metadata, and text metadata. These tests need no AWS and no network. The second layer is a handler suite with moto-mocked S3 and DynamoDB. It invokes lambda_handler with synthetic S3 events, verifies records, and exercises duplicate delivery, malformed events, conditional writes, transient errors, and log behavior. The third layer is the deployed acceptance run documented by the console captures, the DynamoDB scan, the CloudWatch log views, and the SQS envelope.

The layers answer different questions. The unit and handler suites answer whether the repository implements the intended logic. The deployed acceptance run answers whether the resources were configured and whether specific inputs produced specific records. Neither layer substitutes for the other. A moto test passing does not prove that the deployed IAM policy works, and a console screenshot does not prove that an edge case in the validation order is correct.

9.2 Environment and commands#

The local environment is Windows 11, Python 3.13.14, pytest 9.1.1, moto 5.2.4, and Ruff 0.17.0. The test command is python -m pytest -q, and the lint command is python -m ruff check src tests. The dependency check is python -m pip check. The handler tests set dummy AWS credentials and a region in tests/conftest.py before collection, then reload handler inside mock_aws() so the boto3 clients created at import are intercepted.

The suite was re-run for this case study on 18 October 2026. It collected 135 tests and reported 135 passed in 48.66 seconds. Ruff reported all checks passed. pip check reported no broken requirements. The 16 October build record reported 135 passed in 49.34 seconds, so the result is consistent with the recorded build state. The small timing difference is ordinary machine variation.

9.3 Functional testing#

Functional testing covered the happy path for each supported type: JPEG, PNG, and UTF-8 text. The handler tests build a versioned object in moto S3, invoke the handler with a synthetic event, and read the resulting DynamoDB item. The assertions check the record identity, status, file name, file type, file size, SHA-256, metadata, timestamps, and the absence of an error map on success. The deployed acceptance run produced matching COMPLETED records for sample.jpg, sample.png, sample.txt, and images.jpg.

The functional tests also cover uppercase extensions, nested keys, URL-encoded keys, and a multi-record batch with a permanent failure and a success. The URL decoding tests include %20, a literal plus, and %2B, which confirms that unquote_plus behaves as intended. The nested-key tests cover incoming/2026/photo.jpg and incoming/users/demo/file.txt. The deployed positive suite adds 06-nested-image.jpg in a nested/ folder.

9.4 Positive file-validation testing#

The deployed positive suite contains six files: 01-landscape.jpg, 02-portrait.jpeg, 03-square.png, 04-multiline.txt, 05-unicode.txt, and 06-nested-image.jpg. The owner reports that all six completed successfully. The DynamoDB scan corroborates the status for each file: the rows show no error map and the file names match. Figure 9.3 shows the positive folder listing, including the nested/ folder. Figures 9.4 to 9.7 show the corresponding completed records.

The initial acceptance set adds sample.jpg, sample.png, and sample.txt. The scan contains COMPLETED records for all three, plus images.jpg. The sample.png file appears twice because a second version was uploaded for the oversized-dimension test; the smaller version completed and the larger version failed. This is the versioning behavior described in Chapter 4, not a duplicate processing bug.

9.5 Negative file-validation testing#

The deployed negative suite contains six files: 07-empty.txt, 08-unsupported.csv, 09-invalid-utf8.txt, 10-fake-jpeg.jpg, 11-corrupt-png.png, and 12-over-pixel-limit.png. The owner reports that each produced its expected validation error. The DynamoDB scan corroborates the FAILED status and the presence of an error map for each row. The console table truncates the error value, so the exact error_code is not legible in the screenshots. The expected codes follow directly from the validation order: ZERO_BYTE, UNSUPPORTED_EXTENSION, INVALID_ENCODING, TYPE_MISMATCH, CORRUPT_IMAGE, and IMAGE_DIMENSIONS_EXCEEDED.

The initial negative set adds sample.pdf and the zero-byte folder markers. The PDF is 1.6 MB and is rejected before download with UNSUPPORTED_EXTENSION. The folder markers are zero-byte objects created when the console folders were made; they fail with ZERO_BYTE. The scan shows seven such records with an empty file name. They are a useful bonus test of the zero-byte path, and they explain a large part of the failed-record count.

9.6 Nested-path testing#

Nested-path support is covered at three levels. The unit-level handler test invokes incoming/2026/photo.jpg and incoming/users/demo/file.txt.
