The deployed positive suite includes a nested/ folder and a 06-nested-image.jpg record that completed. The S3 trigger uses the incoming/ prefix, which applies to all nested keys under it. The scan row for 06-nested-image has no error map, so the deployed path handling worked for that file. The exact full key is not visible in the truncated table, which is why the document refers to the nested folder and the file name rather than asserting the complete key string.

9.7 Error-handling testing#

The handler suite covers the error paths that matter for correct operation. A malformed event with a missing or null version ID raises and writes nothing. A missing bucket or key raises and writes nothing. A non-string identity field raises and writes nothing, including numeric, boolean, list, object, and null values. A claim failure raises an InfrastructureError and writes nothing. A HeadObject service error writes FAILED with INFRASTRUCTURE and raises. A terminal COMPLETED update failure writes FAILED and raises. A secondary failure is logged and the safe exception is raised. An unexpected image processor exception writes FAILED with INFRASTRUCTURE and does not leak the raw message. A multi-record batch stops at the first infrastructure failure and leaves earlier COMPLETED records intact.

The error truncation tests use a 5,000-character validation message and a long untrusted message with quotes and backslashes. The serialized error must stay within 1,024 characters, the error_code and error_type must remain intact, and the message must be truncated rather than the classification. The redaction tests use a marker string and a chained cause; the marker must not appear in the persisted error, the emitted JSON, or the rendered uncaught exception.

9.8 DynamoDB verification#

The deployed DynamoDB scan returned 25 items and scanned 25 items with 100 percent efficiency and 2.5 RCUs consumed. The item count is the first thing to interpret correctly. It is not a count of 25 independent test scenarios. The 25 records comprise 10 COMPLETED and 15 FAILED records, and several records belong to the same logical test. Table 9.2 breaks down the composition.

The scan rows show the processing_id, bucket, created_at, error, file_name, and file_size columns. The error column is truncated, so the screenshots prove FAILED status and an error map rather than the exact code. The timestamps show that the records cluster on 18 October 2026, which matches the test window. The table does not show metadata, sha256, or processed_at in these column views, so those attributes are verified by the automated tests and the record schema, not by the screenshots.

9.9 CloudWatch verification#

The CloudWatch log group exists and contains seven recent log streams. The log event views show the Lambda platform START, END, and REPORT lines plus application JSON lines. The visible application lines include a PROCESSING start, a permanent validation failure terminal line, and the corresponding END and REPORT lines. The JSON field values are truncated by the console width, so the capture proves the line format and the status values rather than every field value. The log group page does not show the retention setting; 30-day retention is documented but not visually verified.

The captured REPORT durations for the failed invocations are 48.11, 53.69, 104.64, and 339.63 ms across the two log views. These are observations, not benchmarks. They show that a validation failure can complete quickly and that invocation overhead varies. They do not describe successful image processing, and they are not averages.

9.10 SQS and retry verification#

An infrastructure failure was intentionally triggered by changing the function's TABLE_NAME to a table the execution role cannot access. The role is scoped to sfps-processing, so the targeted call fails with an authorization error rather than a resource-not-found error. The handler logs sanitized diagnostics and raises the fixed InfrastructureError. Lambda retries the function error, and after the retries are exhausted the event is delivered to sfps-failed-events.

The captured queue page shows one message available and one received message with receive count 1. The captured message body has condition RetriesExhausted, approximateInvokeCount 3, the original event under requestPayload for incoming/images.jpg, and a responsePayload containing the fixed message and a stack trace that stops at the handler boundary. This confirms the destination behavior for that injected failure. It does not prove that every possible failure mode produces the same envelope, and it does not prove that the retry timing matches a particular schedule.

The same file name, images.jpg, also appears as a COMPLETED record in the DynamoDB scan. The evidence does not establish whether that completion came from a replay, a new upload, or a retry after the configuration was restored. The document therefore describes the two pieces of evidence separately and does not assert an order that the captures do not show.

9.11 Deployment configuration verification#

The console captures verify the function runtime, architecture, memory, timeout, environment variables, trigger prefix and event type, SQS destination, log group existence, IAM role page, and the DynamoDB table browser. The captures do not verify the bucket policy text, the lifecycle rule, the public-access settings, the encryption setting, the exact IAM policy document, the log retention value, the async retry count, or the queue retention and visibility settings. Those are documented configuration items with no direct visual proof in the supplied evidence. The deployment guide contains the commands and console paths to check them.

9.12 Resource-boundary testing#

The repository includes boundary tests for the size limit, the pixel budget, and the text counters. The handler accepts an object exactly at the 25 MiB limit and rejects one byte over. The image validator accepts a 4000 by 4000 PNG and rejects a 4001 by 4000 PNG. An animated PNG budget test counts every frame canvas. A 12,000 by 12,000 PNG is rejected before decode with IMAGE_DIMENSIONS_EXCEEDED. A 200,000-line text fixture is counted with less than 1 MiB of extra allocation. These tests ran locally on Windows Python 3.13.14.

The local boundary tests do not certify the deployed Lambda memory or timeout. The build state explicitly says that host measurements are not Linux arm64 Lambda metrics. The deployed oversized-image case is observed as a FAILED record, but the 25 MiB text case and the exact pixel-boundary image case were not measured on the deployed function in the supplied evidence. That remains an outstanding acceptance item.

9.13 Performance observations#

Performance evidence is limited. The most specific observation is a single successful PNG invocation recorded by the owner at 89 ms of application processing, 150.13 ms of Lambda execution, and 117 MB of peak memory against a 512 MB configuration. The 89 ms figure is the handler's processing_duration; the 150.13 ms figure is the Lambda REPORT duration. They measure different intervals and should not be added or averaged together.

The failed-invocation REPORT durations visible in CloudWatch range from 48.11 ms to 339.63 ms. The variation is consistent with different validation paths, cold versus warm execution environments, and normal service overhead. The evidence does not include a controlled cold start study, a throughput test, a concurrency test, or a 25 MiB boundary measurement. The case study does not present these numbers as a benchmark.

9.14 Deployed test matrix#

9.15 Automated and boundary test matrix#

9.16 Test status and remaining gaps#

The automated suite is comprehensive for the handler and pure modules. The deployed evidence is strong for the resource topology, the positive and negative acceptance files, the DynamoDB records, the CloudWatch log format, and one injected SQS failure. The evidence is weaker for the exact IAM policy attachment, the bucket configuration pages, the log retention value, the async retry count, and the 25 MiB memory and timeout boundary. The case study marks those as implemented but not independently verified rather than filling the gaps with assumptions.

Three tests remain outstanding for a full acceptance close-out. First, measure a 25 MiB text file and a pixel-boundary image on the deployed function and record REPORT memory and duration. Second, capture the bucket Properties and Permissions pages plus the attached IAM policy JSON. Third, capture the log group retention setting and the asynchronous invocation retry count. Those captures would convert several documented items into visually verified evidence.

CHAPTER 10

Results and Performance Analysis

10.1 Evidence summary#

The results come from three sources: the repository test suite, the deployed console captures, and the captured SQS envelope. The test suite establishes the behavior of the code under controlled inputs. The console captures establish that the resources exist and that the acceptance files produced records. The envelope establishes that one infrastructure failure exhausted retries and reached the SQS destination. The results below separate those sources instead of blending them into a single success claim.

10.2 Processing results#

The deployed acceptance run produced COMPLETED records for the initial JPEG, PNG, and text files, plus images.jpg. The additional positive suite produced COMPLETED records for all six files: 01-landscape.jpg, 02-portrait.jpeg, 03-square.png, 04-multiline.txt, 05-unicode.txt, and 06-nested-image.jpg. The DynamoDB scan shows no error map on those rows. The record names and sizes match the S3 listings where both are visible. This is the strongest end-to-end evidence in the project: an upload became an event, the event became a function invocation, and the invocation became a durable record.

The table also contains a COMPLETED record for sample.png with a smaller size and a FAILED record for sample.png with a larger size. The two records are different S3 versions of the same key. The completed version passed validation; the larger version exceeded the pixel budget. This is the versioned-identity model working as designed. The same bytes did not receive two different outcomes.

10.3 Validation results#

The deployed negative suite produced FAILED records for all six files. The initial negative set produced FAILED records for sample.pdf and the larger sample.png version. The seven zero-byte folder markers also produced FAILED records. The FAILED records carry an error map; the console table truncates the map, so the screenshots confirm failure and the presence of an error rather than the exact code. The owner-reported results and the validation order support the expected codes: ZERO_BYTE, UNSUPPORTED_EXTENSION, INVALID_ENCODING, TYPE_MISMATCH, CORRUPT_IMAGE, and IMAGE_DIMENSIONS_EXCEEDED.

The failure classification behaved as intended at the batch level. The permanent failures did not loop. The initial acceptance set returned successfully even though it contained a PDF and zero-byte markers. The SQS queue did not receive those permanent failures. The one captured SQS message came from an intentionally injected infrastructure failure, which is the correct channel for that class of error.

10.4 State persistence and metadata#

The DynamoDB scan shows the processing_id, bucket, created_at, file_name, file_size, and error columns. It does not show sha256, metadata, processed_at, or the full error map in the captured views. The automated tests verify the full record shape for JPEG, PNG, and text, including the exact metadata dictionaries and SHA-256 values. The deployed screenshots verify that the records were written and that the statuses are correct. The combination supports the schema and the persistence behavior without pretending that every attribute is visible in a console table.

The automated text tests assert that a trailing newline does not add a line, that whitespace-only text has zero words, that Unicode counts code points rather than bytes, and that CRLF is handled. The image tests assert exact width, height, and format for JPEG and PNG. The handler tests assert that these metadata dictionaries are stored under the metadata attribute and that the checksum matches hashlib.sha256 over the same bytes. The deployed records are consistent with those contracts.

10.5 Nested-path support#

The positive suite includes a nested/ folder and a 06-nested-image.jpg record. The record completed with no error map. The handler unit tests also cover incoming/2026/photo.jpg and incoming/users/demo/file.txt. The S3 trigger's incoming/ prefix applies to all nested keys. The combination verifies that the deployed pipeline is not limited to a flat upload folder.

10.6 Versioning behavior#

The two sample.png records demonstrate the versioning behavior in the deployed table. The smaller version completed; the larger version failed. The record identity includes the version ID, so the two versions do not collide. The SQS envelope also carries a versionId for images.jpg, which confirms that the event payload includes the version field the handler requires. The lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 30 days is documented but not visible in the captures.

10.7 CloudWatch observations#

The log group contains seven recent streams. The captured log events show the platform START, END, and REPORT lines and application JSON lines. The application lines carry the status field and a message. The JSON values are truncated by the console width, so the full object_key, version_id, and error fields are not legible in the capture. The log format is verified; the complete field values are not. The application logger's non-propagation behavior and its sanitized exception rendering are verified by tests rather than by the console view.

The REPORT durations in the captured failed invocations are 48.11, 53.69, 104.64, and 339.63 ms. These numbers are useful for showing that the function returns quickly on a validation failure. They are not a throughput measurement, a cold-start measurement, or a successful image-processing benchmark. The variation may come from execution environment reuse, validation path differences, or normal service overhead. The evidence does not isolate those factors.

10.8 Performance observations#

The single recorded successful PNG invocation is the most specific performance observation in the project. The owner recorded 89 ms of application processing, 150.13 ms of Lambda execution, and 117 MB of peak memory against a 512 MB configuration. The application duration is measured by the handler around the processing pipeline. The Lambda duration is measured by the platform around the invocation. The memory figure is the platform's peak for that invocation. One invocation does not establish an average, a percentile, or a capacity plan.

The local measurements are included because they explain why the resource bounds were added. The 25 MiB text case previously used 548.8 MiB of working set under the list-based implementation; the iterator-based implementation reduced it to 69.4 MiB. That is a meaningful engineering result, but it was measured on Windows, not on the deployed Linux arm64 function. The case study does not convert it into a Lambda guarantee.

10.9 Reliability behavior#

The captured SQS envelope is the strongest reliability evidence. It shows that an injected infrastructure failure produced a RetriesExhausted condition, an approximate invoke count of 3, the original event under requestPayload, and a sanitized responsePayload. That is the expected behavior for a function error that exhausts the asynchronous retry budget. The queue page shows one message available and one received message with receive count 1. The message was not deleted in the capture, which is consistent with the absence of a consumer.

The automated tests provide complementary reliability evidence: duplicate delivery is skipped, PROCESSING is re-attempted, a terminal race does not overwrite a completed record, a malformed event writes nothing, a HeadObject error becomes a FAILED infrastructure record, and a secondary failure is logged without replacing the original diagnostic. These tests use moto, so they do not prove the deployed IAM or network behavior. They do prove the handler's state machine and error classification.

10.10 Claims not made#

The project does not claim that the deployed function meets a particular latency service level, that it sustains a particular request rate, that it is cheaper than a server-based worker at the project's actual volume, or that it has been tested against malicious files beyond the listed fixtures. It does not claim that the validation is exhaustive for every malformed image or Unicode edge case. It does not claim that the error codes visible in the console are complete for every record, because the table view truncates them. It does not claim that the system is production-ready without the enhancements in Chapter 13.

CHAPTER 11

Challenges and Solutions

The project produced several engineering difficulties that were not obvious from the requirements alone. Each one changed the implementation or the documentation. The sections below describe the cause, the investigation, the resolution, and the lesson. Only issues that appear in the repository history, the build state, or the deployment evidence are included.

11.1 Packaging Linux ARM64 dependencies from Windows#

The build host is Windows and the Lambda target is Linux arm64. A normal pip install on the host resolves Windows wheels, including Windows .pyd extension modules for Pillow. Those modules cannot load on Lambda. The investigation compared the target runtime (Python 3.13 on Amazon Linux 2023, arm64) with the host platform and identified the need for a cross-platform wheel download. The resolution uses pip's --python-version, --implementation, --abi, --platform, and --only-binary options to fetch manylinux_2_28_aarch64 cp313 wheels. The lesson is that a deployment package is a target artifact, not a copy of the developer environment.

11.2 Lambda ZIP archive layout#

Lambda imports the handler by module path. A ZIP that contains a top-level src/ folder puts handler.py at src/handler.py, which does not match handler.lambda_handler. A ZIP built with PowerShell 5.1 Compress-Archive can also contain backslash entry names that Lambda cannot unpack. The investigation reproduced both failure modes in the packaging checks. The resolution copies the contents of src/ into a flat build directory, zips the contents with Python's zipfile, replaces os.sep with a forward slash, and asserts that handler.py is at the root, no entry contains a backslash, and no entry starts with ./. The lesson is that archive layout is part of the application contract.

11.3 S3 versioning and version-pinned reads#

Versioning is required for the processing identity, but it also changes how reads must be performed. An event refers to a specific version. If the handler calls GetObject without a version ID, it may read a newer object than the event described. The investigation tied the processing identity to the version ID and added VersionId to both HeadObject and GetObject. A missing or null version ID is now a malformed event. The lesson is that an event's identity must travel with every read that depends on it.

11.4 IAM permission scope#

An early deployment can fail with AccessDenied if the policy ARNs still contain placeholders or if the S3 resource is scoped to the bucket ARN without the incoming/ prefix. The investigation compared each policy statement with the actual resource ARN and the operations the handler performs. The resolution uses a prefix-scoped S3 resource, a table-scoped DynamoDB resource, a queue ARN for SendMessage, and a log-group ARN with the :* suffix. The lesson is that a policy is only least-privilege if its resource scope matches the code's actual access pattern.

11.5 Zero-byte folder markers#

Creating a folder in the S3 console creates a zero-byte object whose key ends with a slash. Those objects match the incoming/ prefix and invoke the function. The first reaction is to treat them as noise. The investigation showed that they are valid S3 objects and that the pipeline should record them rather than ignore them. The resolution keeps the zero-byte check before the extension check, so a folder marker becomes FAILED with ZERO_BYTE. The result is seven documented folder-marker records in the scan. The lesson is that console conveniences create real objects, and the pipeline's behavior should be predictable for them.

11.6 Handling unsupported extensions#

An unsupported file must not disappear silently. A suffix filter on the S3 notification would prevent a PDF from reaching Lambda, but it would also remove any record of the rejection. The resolution uses no suffix filter and checks the extension allowlist after the size check and before the content download. The PDF becomes a FAILED record with UNSUPPORTED_EXTENSION and does not consume bandwidth for its 1.6 MB body. The lesson is that observability sometimes requires accepting an event you intend to reject.

11.7 Detecting fake or corrupt images#

An extension check is not enough. A file named .jpg can contain PNG bytes, text, or a truncated JPEG. The investigation added a signature check, a Pillow verify pass, a reopen, and a full decode of every frame. A signature mismatch becomes TYPE_MISMATCH; a matching signature that cannot be verified or decoded becomes CORRUPT_IMAGE. The regression suite includes a PNG with a damaged IDAT checksum and a truncated JPEG. The lesson is that image validation needs both a cheap signature check and a real decoder pass.

11.8 Oversized image validation#

A small file can decode into a very large pixel buffer. The investigation found a 420 KB PNG that exceeded 512 MiB when decoded. The resolution adds a total-pixel budget of 16,000,000 across all frame canvases, checked before allocation. A 12,000 by 12,000 PNG is rejected before decode. Animated PNGs are covered because the budget multiplies by the frame count. The lesson is that upload size is not a proxy for decode cost.

11.9 UTF-8 decoding failures#

Text files can contain invalid byte sequences. A permissive decode would replace them with replacement characters and produce misleading counts. The resolution uses strict UTF-8 decode, maps failures to INVALID_ENCODING, and strips exactly one leading BOM after a successful decode. A BOM-only file becomes an empty string and is valid at the text layer; a zero-byte object is rejected earlier. The lesson is that text statistics are only meaningful after a strict decode.

11.10 Asynchronous retry troubleshooting#

An asynchronous invocation failure is not visible in the same way as a synchronous request. The function's exception is logged, but the retry and destination behavior is controlled by Lambda. The investigation used the SQS destination envelope to confirm the condition and invoke count. The captured message shows RetriesExhausted and approximateInvokeCount 3. The resolution is a documented failure-injection procedure: point TABLE_NAME at a table the role cannot access, upload a supported file, wait for retries, inspect the queue, then restore the variable. The lesson is that retry behavior must be observed at the destination, not inferred from a function log alone.

11.11 Distinguishing validation failures from infrastructure exceptions#

The first failure model treated every exception as retryable. That would turn a corrupt image into an endless retry loop. The investigation separated ValidationError from unexpected exceptions, added a guarded FAILED write, and moved the fixed boundary error to the top of the handler. The resolution makes a validation failure return successfully and an infrastructure failure raise. The lesson is that retry semantics are a property of the error class, not a global policy.

11.12 Evidence drift and stale build artifacts#

The workspace contains an older build/ directory with botocore 1.43.113, while the verified function.zip contains 1.43.112. A casual review could describe the wrong package. The investigation compared the archive metadata with requirements.txt and treated function.zip as the release artifact. The resolution documents the stale directory and cites the archive, not the working directory. The lesson is that evidence has a provenance, and the newest-looking folder is not always the released artifact.

CHAPTER 12

Cost and Operational Considerations

12.1 Pay-per-use model#

Every service in the pipeline is pay-per-use. There is no idle server, no provisioned database capacity, and no reserved concurrency. The cost is driven by the number and size of uploaded objects, the duration and memory of each Lambda invocation, the number of DynamoDB reads and writes, the number of SQS messages, and the volume of logs retained. The project did not collect billing data, so this chapter describes the cost model qualitatively. It does not present dollar figures.

The acceptance workload was tiny: a few dozen uploads, a handful of image decodes, and a small number of log lines. Any real bill for that workload would be dominated by rounding, free-tier allowances, or the minimum billable units rather than by the architecture. A numeric cost claim without a billing export would be misleading.

12.2 Amazon S3#

S3 charges for storage, requests, and data transfer. The project stores small source files and keeps current versions indefinitely plus noncurrent versions for 30 days. The main cost drivers are the number and size of stored versions, the number of PUT and GET requests, and any data transfer out of the region. The function's reads are version-pinned GET and HEAD requests. The bucket has no public website endpoint, so there is no public transfer path.

The lifecycle rule is a cost control as well as a retention control. Expiring noncurrent versions after 30 days prevents repeated uploads from accumulating storage indefinitely. It does not delete current versions, so the latest object for each key remains available.

12.3 AWS Lambda#

Lambda charges for the number of requests and for compute duration multiplied by the configured memory. The function runs at 512 MB with a 30-second timeout. The observed failed validation invocations completed in tens to hundreds of milliseconds. The one recorded successful PNG invocation used 150.13 ms of Lambda duration and 117 MB of peak memory. The memory setting is the billing lever: a higher setting can finish sooner but costs more per millisecond; a lower setting may take longer or fail on larger images.

Asynchronous retries can multiply the invocation count for a failing event. A persistent infrastructure failure can consume the initial attempt plus two function-error retries, and throttling or system errors can add more retries up to the maximum event age. The SQS destination itself is not a Lambda charge, but the extra invocations are. This is one reason the failure classification matters for cost as well as correctness.

12.4 Amazon DynamoDB#

The table uses on-demand capacity, so the project pays per read and write request unit rather than for provisioned capacity. Each record involves a conditional PutItem, possibly a GetItem after a claim conflict, and a conditional UpdateItem. The scan used for verification is a table scan and consumes read capacity proportional to the number and size of items. A production workload would use targeted queries or a secondary index instead of repeated scans.

The table has no TTL, so records accumulate. That is appropriate for an operational ledger, but it is a cost consideration over time. A future retention policy could archive or expire old records. The project does not enable point-in-time recovery, which avoids the PITR storage cost but also removes a recovery option.

12.5 Amazon SQS#

SQS charges per request, with a free tier for standard queues. The queue receives messages only when an asynchronous invocation exhausts its retries, so the request volume is expected to be low in normal operation. The 14-day retention keeps a failed message available for investigation without an immediate consumer. A production design would add a consumer or an alert, which would add its own request and compute cost.

12.6 Amazon CloudWatch Logs#

CloudWatch Logs charges for ingestion and storage. The application writes one JSON start line and one terminal line per record, plus diagnostic lines for failures. The Lambda platform adds START, END, and REPORT lines. The 30-day retention bounds storage growth. A high-volume workload would want a log-level policy, structured filtering, and possibly a shorter retention for verbose diagnostics. The project keeps INFO logging and 30-day retention as a simple operational baseline.

12.7 Cost drivers#

12.8 No billing evidence#

The project did not export Cost Explorer data, a billing report, or a budget. The case study therefore does not state an actual monthly cost, a cost per file, or a comparison with a server-based alternative. Those claims would require a measured workload and a billing period. The qualitative model is enough to explain what would drive the bill and which design choices bound it.

12.9 Operational considerations#

The operational burden is mostly configuration and observation. The manual deployment requires careful ARN replacement, a pre-created log group, and a versioning propagation wait. Once deployed, the routine checks are the DynamoDB table for FAILED records, CloudWatch for diagnostic lines, and SQS for unexpected messages. There is no server to patch, but there are managed-service quotas, runtime deprecation dates, and dependency updates to track. A production operation would add alarms, a runbook, and a replay procedure before it could claim a meaningful service level.

CHAPTER 13

Limitations and Future Enhancements

13.1 Current limitations#

V1 is a manual deployment. There is no infrastructure as code, no CI/CD pipeline, and no automated environment promotion. The function handles four file extensions and does not process PDFs, video, archives, or office documents. It does not resize images, scan for malware, deduplicate content by checksum, or enrich metadata beyond dimensions and text counts. It does not use a DynamoDB transaction, a dead-letter queue for SQS, or a consumer that replays failed events.

The observability is basic. There are no CloudWatch alarms, dashboards, or metric filters. A message in the failure queue is visible only if an operator looks. The table has no point-in-time recovery and no secondary indexes. The function has no reserved concurrency. The deployment package is built and uploaded by hand. The 25 MiB memory and timeout boundary has not been measured on the deployed function. The IAM policy and bucket configuration are documented but not all of their values are visually verified in the captures.

13.2 Future enhancements#

The most valuable next step is infrastructure as code. A SAM or Terraform definition would make the bucket, table, queue, role, function, trigger, destination, and log group reproducible and reviewable. It would also remove the placeholder-replacement errors that manual deployment invites. A CI/CD pipeline could run the test suite, build the arm64 package, and deploy to a staging account after approval. The current repository is already structured for that: the tests are offline, the package build is scripted, and the configuration is explicit.

The second step is operational monitoring. CloudWatch alarms on Lambda errors, throttles, duration, and SQS visible messages would turn a silent failure into a notification. A metric filter on the application FAILED status could separate validation failures from infrastructure failures. A dashboard could show uploads, completions, rejections, and queue depth. A replay tool could read a failure envelope, verify that the original event is well formed, and invoke the function asynchronously after the cause is fixed.

The third step is broader validation and load testing. The boundary tests should run on the deployed function with a 25 MiB text file and a pixel-boundary image, recording REPORT memory and duration. A concurrency test could measure how the function behaves when many objects arrive at once. A fuzzing pass could feed malformed image headers, truncated text, and unusual Unicode. A cost test could compare on-demand DynamoDB with a provisioned or adaptive baseline for a realistic workload.

Feature enhancements could add PDF text extraction, image thumbnails, malware scanning, or content deduplication. Each adds a new validation surface, a new dependency, and a new failure mode. They should follow the same pattern as the current types: a signature or structure check, a bounded decode, a fixed metadata schema, and a clear error taxonomy. Adding formats without those controls would weaken the design.

13.3 Prioritized roadmap#

13.4 What is not planned#

The project does not plan to add a web frontend, API Gateway, Cognito, CloudFront, Step Functions, SNS notifications, or a container image for V1. Those services could be useful in a different product, but they would distract from the processing pipeline and the evidence. The same applies to multi-region replication and a full observability platform. The roadmap prioritizes the controls that make the existing pipeline reproducible and observable.

CHAPTER 14

Conclusion and Lessons Learned

14.1 Demonstrated outcomes#

SFPS demonstrates a complete event-driven file-processing pipeline on AWS. An upload to a private, versioned S3 bucket invokes a Python 3.13 Lambda function. The function validates the file, extracts metadata, computes a SHA-256 checksum, and writes one deterministic DynamoDB record per object version. Structured JSON logs go to CloudWatch. Permanent validation failures become FAILED records and do not retry. Infrastructure failures are retried and, when the retries are exhausted, delivered to an SQS queue. The deployed evidence includes a 25-item DynamoDB scan with 10 COMPLETED and 15 FAILED records, a captured SQS envelope with RetriesExhausted and approximateInvokeCount 3, and a single successful PNG invocation at 89 ms of application time, 150.13 ms of Lambda time, and 117 MB of peak memory.

The project also demonstrates the engineering discipline around the pipeline. The repository contains 135 automated tests, a clean Ruff run, a dependency lock, a verified Linux arm64 deployment archive, a product requirements document, an architecture decision log, a build state, a console deployment guide, and this evidence-backed case study. The claims are separated by evidence layer, and the gaps are named rather than hidden.

14.2 Design decisions that mattered#

Four decisions carried most of the design. The deterministic processing identity made idempotency possible without a separate deduplication service. The version-pinned read made the record describe the bytes that were actually processed. The conditional write protocol made concurrent and duplicate invocations safe. The failure classification kept expected rejections out of the retry loop while preserving a path for genuine operational faults. Each decision is small in code and large in consequence.

A fifth decision was to keep the pure logic separate from AWS orchestration. The validation, checksum, and processor modules do not import boto3. That separation made the unit tests fast and focused, and it made the handler tests about orchestration rather than decoding. The project structure is not elaborate, but the seam is in the right place.

14.3 Reliability lessons#

The project reinforced a few lessons that apply beyond AWS. At-least-once delivery is the default assumption, not an edge case. A retry policy must be tied to the error class. A record should identify the exact input it processed, including its version, rather than its file name alone. A build artifact needs provenance, because a working directory can contain stale dependencies. A console screenshot proves only what it shows; the rest is documentation, and the difference should be stated.

The evidence gaps are part of the result. The 25 MiB memory and timeout boundary, the attached IAM policy, the bucket configuration pages, and the log retention value are not fully verified in the supplied captures. Naming those gaps is more useful than filling them with confident prose. A reviewer can run the remaining checks with the deployment guide, and the case study will still be accurate.

14.4 Final assessment#

SFPS is a credible V1 serverless file-processing system. It handles the supported formats, records every object version, separates expected rejections from operational faults, and produces enough evidence to audit the main claims. It is a well-scoped engineering project rather than a production platform, and it shows how the pieces fit together and where the next layer of work would go.

The most useful outcome is the habit of asking what each claim rests on, more than the list of AWS services. The repository tests, the deployed captures, the SQS envelope, and the owner-recorded metrics each answer a different question. Keeping those answers separate is what makes the project defensible.
